title: The circle check-in: everyone speaks once
description: Before a family discussion or a group decision, go around the circle: each person speaks once, briefly, with no interruptions, before anyone speaks twice. It changes what gets heard.

body.heading: How the circle runs
paragraphs: Sit where everyone can see everyone else. Choose one question — 'What should we do about…?' or simply 'How is everyone, really?' Go around in order; each person gets up to a minute, and nobody may interrupt, correct or answer during someone else's turn.
Only when every voice has been heard once does open discussion begin. The person who suggested the question speaks last in the first round, so their view does not anchor everyone else's.

body.heading: Why it works
paragraphs: In open discussion, the fastest talkers set the agenda and quieter people edit themselves out. The circle guarantees the quietest person the same first minute as the loudest — and knowing your turn is coming makes listening easier, because you are not fighting for a gap.
Keep it short and use it often: a weekly family circle of ten minutes surfaces small problems while they are still small.

takeaway: Go once around the circle with no interruptions before open discussion — everyone gets a first minute, so everyone gets heard.
materials: A circle of chairs or cushions
A timer or phone clock for one-minute turns
supervision: One person facilitates: they keep time, protect each turn from interruption and speak last in the first round.
safetyNotes: Anyone may pass on a question that feels too personal — passing is always allowed and never questioned.
What is shared in the circle stays in the circle unless the speaker says otherwise.
